plan: Eleven new items, Expression of Ideas weighted up; harder vocabulary in less familiar senses (pointed, qualify), a two-part data claim, a mechanism inference, and an apparent-exception function item.

passages.title: Senator speech
passages.text: Observers who expected a conciliatory address were surprised: the senator's speech was ______ from start to finish, naming each of her opponents and listing what she saw as their failures one by one.

passages.title: Drug trial in mice
passages.text: Though the drug's effects in mice were striking, the researchers were careful to ______ their findings, noting that the doses the mice received were far higher than any a human patient could safely be given.

passages.title: Commute shares
passages.text:
A city opened a network of protected bike lanes in 2021. The table shows the percentage of the city's commuters using each mode of travel.
Mode | 2019 | 2023
Car | 70% | 62%
Bus | 20% | 20%
Bicycle | 4% | 12%
A city planner claims that the new bike lanes drew riders mainly from people who would otherwise have driven, not from people who would otherwise have taken the bus.

passages.title: Island lizards
passages.text: Biologist Nadia Ferro introduced a ground-hunting predator to six small islands and left six similar islands untouched. Within a year, lizards on the predator islands spent far more time high in shrubs, and those with shorter legs, which grip narrow branches better, survived at higher rates than long-legged lizards. On the untouched islands, leg length had no measurable effect on survival. These results suggest that ______

passages.title: Blue pigment
passages.text: The pigment—made by grinding a blue mineral that was carried by traders from distant mountains ______ was so costly that painters often reserved it for the robes of a painting's most important figures.

passages.title: Glacier survey
passages.text: By the time the survey team finally reached the edge of the glacier, the storm ______ for three days, burying the markers the team had planted the previous season under nearly a meter of fresh snow.

passages.title: Prototypes
passages.text: Neither of the two prototype drones performed as the engineers had hoped. Each lost power well before ______ battery was fully drained, a problem the team later traced to a faulty voltage regulator.

passages.title: Chemist yield
passages.text: For months, chemist Lucia Ramos's experiments produced only trace amounts of the compound. ______ she noticed that the yield rose sharply whenever the reaction vessel sat near a sunny window, a clue that light was driving the reaction.

passages.title: Bridge notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Halden Bridge and the Morrow Bridge are suspension bridges.
• The Halden Bridge is 1,240 meters long.
• It was completed in 1931.
• The Morrow Bridge is 980 meters long.
• It was completed in 1937.

passages.title: Bee notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ecologist Mara Quist studied bumblebees in 40 city gardens.
• She counted bee visits to native and non-native flowers.
• Native flowers received about three times as many visits.
• Quist concluded that planting native flowers could help support urban bumblebee populations.

passages.title: Cholera map
passages.text: In the 1850s, many physicians in London held that cholera spread through foul air. During an 1854 outbreak, physician John Snow mapped the homes of those who died and found that they clustered around a single public water pump. Workers at a nearby brewery, who drank the beer they were given rather than water from the pump, were largely spared. Snow's findings pointed to contaminated water, not air, as the source.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: naming each of her opponents and listing what she saw as their failures one by one
candidates.explanation: A speech that names opponents and lists their failures is sharply critical and direct: "pointed." It contrasts with the conciliatory address observers expected.

A.rationale: "Measured" means restrained, close to the conciliatory tone the speech did not have.

C.rationale: "Rambling" means unfocused, but listing failures one by one is organized.

D.rationale: "Eloquent" describes skill with words, not the critical, direct quality the colon describes.

hints: What was expected, and how did the speech differ?
What does the clause after the colon describe?
candidates.remember: Some words, like "pointed," have a less familiar meaning.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: noting that the doses the mice received were far higher than any a human patient could safely be given
candidates.explanation: The researchers add a limitation (the doses were unrealistically high), which is what it means to "qualify" a finding: to restrict or temper it.

A.rationale: Pointing out a limitation is the opposite of promoting the findings.

B.rationale: Repeating the experiment is a reasonable step, but the sentence describes a caution, not a repetition.

D.rationale: "Careful" and the noted limitation point away from overstating.

hints: What do the researchers point out about the doses?
Which word means to limit or temper a claim?

strategy.explanation: Predict "limit" or "add a caveat to," then match.

candidates.remember: "Qualify" can mean to limit a statement.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the planner's claim?

choices.A: In both 2019 and 2023, a majority of commuters drove, while a fifth of commuters took the bus.
choices.B: The bicycle share was below the bus share in 2019 and also remained below it in 2023.
choices.C: The share of commuters who biked in 2023 was three times the share who biked in 2019.
choices.D: From 2019 to 2023, the bicycle share rose 8 points as the car share fell 8 points and the bus share held steady.

candidates.evidence: drew riders mainly from people who would otherwise have driven
candidates.explanation: The claim links the bike gain to drivers, not bus riders. D shows the bicycle gain matched the car loss while the bus share did not move.

A.rationale: Both statements are true but say nothing about where new cyclists came from.

B.rationale: This is true but compares levels, not the source of new riders.

C.rationale: Bike growth alone does not show whether riders came from cars or buses.

hints: The claim has two parts: from cars, and not from buses.
Which choice addresses both?

strategy.explanation: Break the claim into parts and check each choice against both.

candidates.remember: Support must address every part of the claim.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the predator affected which lizards survived mainly by changing where the lizards spent their time.
choices.B: shorter legs helped the lizards outrun the ground-hunting predator when they were caught in the open.
choices.C: long-legged lizards were more likely than short-legged lizards to be eaten on both kinds of islands.
choices.D: the lizards on the untouched islands would also soon come to have shorter legs, on average.

candidates.evidence: those with shorter legs, which grip narrow branches better, survived at higher rates
candidates.explanation: The predator pushed lizards into shrubs, where short legs help grip branches, and leg length mattered only on predator islands. So the predator's effect on survival worked through the change in habitat use.

B.rationale: The text says short legs help grip branches, not run; it never describes outrunning the predator.

C.rationale: On untouched islands leg length had no effect on survival.

D.rationale: Nothing on the untouched islands favored short legs, so there is no basis for this prediction.

hints: Why did short legs help on predator islands?
Did leg length matter where there was no predator?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that contradict the untouched-island result or the branch-gripping detail.

candidates.remember: Find the mechanism the text describes, not one you supply.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The interrupting phrase opens with a dash after "pigment," so it must close with a dash before the verb "was."

A.rationale: A dash-opened interruption must close with a dash, not a comma.

C.rationale: A semicolon would separate the subject "pigment" from its verb "was."

D.rationale: With no closing mark, the interruption runs into the main clause.

hints: How does the interrupting phrase begin?
Where does the main clause resume?

strategy.explanation: Match the closing mark to the opening mark.

candidates.remember: Interruptions close with the same mark that opened them.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: By the time the survey team finally reached the edge of the glacier
candidates.explanation: "By the time ... reached" sets a past reference point; the storm's three days of raging came before it, which calls for the past perfect "had raged."

A.rationale: Present tense clashes with the past-tense "reached."

B.rationale: Future perfect looks forward from a future point, but the events are past.

C.rationale: Present progressive clashes with the past-tense narration.

hints: What tense is "reached"?
Did the storm happen before or after the team arrived?
candidates.remember: "By the time" + past calls for the past perfect.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The pronoun refers to "Each" (each drone), which is singular, so the singular possessive "its" is needed.
hints: What does the pronoun refer to?
Is "Each" singular or plural?

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: After months of poor results, Ramos made a discovery later on: "Eventually" marks the shift in time.

A.rationale: Her noticing the light effect was not caused by the low yields.

C.rationale: The discovery is not an example of the poor results.

D.rationale: The discovery is not similar to the failed experiments.

hints: "For months" sets up what kind of change?

strategy.explanation: Predict "after a long time," then match.

candidates.remember: Time phrases often signal a sequence transition.

candidates.stem: The student wants to compare the lengths of the two bridges while indicating which bridge was completed first. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Halden Bridge, completed in 1931, is longer than the Morrow Bridge, which was completed six years later.
choices.B: The Halden Bridge is 1,240 meters long, while the Morrow Bridge, also a suspension bridge, is 980 meters long.
choices.C: Completed in 1931 and 1937, respectively, the Halden and Morrow Bridges are both long suspension bridges.
choices.D: The Morrow Bridge, which is shorter than the Halden Bridge, is a suspension bridge completed in 1937.

candidates.explanation: A compares the lengths (Halden is longer) and makes the order clear (Morrow was completed six years after Halden).

B.rationale: This compares lengths but gives no completion dates.

C.rationale: This gives both dates but does not compare the lengths.

D.rationale: This compares lengths but gives only the Morrow date, so it does not show which came first.

hints: The goal has two parts: length comparison and order of completion.
Can you tell which came first from each choice?

strategy.explanation: Turn the goal into a two-item checklist.

candidates.remember: Check every part of the goal against each choice.

candidates.stem: The student wants to present the study's conclusion to an audience already familiar with how the study was conducted. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Quist counted bumblebee visits to native and non-native flowers in 40 city gardens.
choices.B: In the 40 gardens, native flowers drew about three times as many bumblebee visits.
choices.C: Quist concluded that planting native flowers could help support city bumblebees.
choices.D: Ecologist Mara Quist studied the bumblebees that visit flowers in city gardens.

candidates.evidence: Quist concluded that planting native flowers could help support urban bumblebee populations.
candidates.explanation: The goal is the conclusion, and the audience already knows the method; C states Quist's conclusion.

A.rationale: This describes the method, which the audience already knows.

B.rationale: This is the finding, not the conclusion Quist drew from it.

D.rationale: This introduces the study rather than presenting its conclusion.

hints: Separate method, result and conclusion in the notes.

strategy.explanation: Identify which note the goal asks for.

candidates.remember: A finding and a conclusion are different notes.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It introduces a second explanation for the outbreak that Snow later considered and rejected.
choices.B: It describes the mapping method that Snow used to determine where the victims had lived.
choices.C: It notes an exception to the pattern on Snow's map that weakens his conclusion about the pump.
choices.D: It presents a case that is hard to explain if the disease spread through air rather than water.

candidates.evidence: who drank the beer they were given rather than water from the pump, were largely spared
candidates.explanation: The brewery workers lived and worked near the pump, breathing the same air, yet avoided its water and were spared. That is difficult for the foul-air theory to explain and supports Snow's water conclusion.

A.rationale: The sentence gives no new explanation; it is evidence about the existing two.

B.rationale: The mapping method is described in the second sentence, not the third.

C.rationale: The workers look like an exception to the cluster, but because they avoided the pump water, they support rather than weaken Snow's conclusion.

hints: What did the brewery workers share with their neighbors, and what didn't they share?
Which theory does that difference support?

strategy.explanation: Ask whether the sentence helps or hurts each theory.

candidates.remember: An apparent exception can be strong evidence for a claim.
